analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal staffing, infection-control, and transparency rules for nursing homes and bans forced arbitration with residents.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action; it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set new federal requirements for the roughly 15,000 nursing homes that care for Medicare and Medicaid patients: a registered nurse on site 24 hours a day, an infection-prevention specialist at least 40 hours a week, minimum staff-to-resident ratios set by regulators, surety bonds of at least $500,000 so facilities can cover failures, and penalties up to $10,000 for submitting false staffing data. It would also ban nursing homes and home-care providers from making residents sign pre-dispute arbitration agreements, and would audit facility cost reports to show where the money actually goes. States that raise nursing home staff wages and benefits would get an extra 1 to 3 percentage points of federal Medicaid money for six years.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home and skilled nursing facility residents, most of whom are elderly, disabled, or on Medicaid, would get stronger minimum care standards, more accurate public data about staffing, and the right to sue in court instead of being forced into arbitration. Nursing home workers would benefit from a six-year boost in federal Medicaid payments that states may use only to raise staff wages and benefits, fund training, and reduce turnover.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and care workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires a registered professional nurse on site 24 hours a day, 7 days a week starting October 2023, up from the previous 8-hour requirement.
Requires infection control services overseen by an infection preventionist for at least 40 hours per week, with rural and small-facility waivers.
Directs CMS to study and then set minimum staff-to-resident ratios for nurses and aides, with waivers for rural facilities.
Prohibits nursing facilities, skilled nursing facilities, and home and community-based care providers from entering into or enforcing pre-dispute arbitration agreements with residents or clients.

Creates civil monetary penalties of up to $10,000 per submission for facilities that report inaccurate staffing data, and cuts Medicare payment rates by 2 percentage points for facilities that submit inaccurate quality data.
Requires annual audits of a sample of nursing facility cost reports, with $250 million in funding, so regulators and the public can see how facilities spend Medicare and Medicaid money.
Requires a surety bond of at least $500,000 from Medicare and Medicaid nursing facilities so funds exist when facilities fail.

Raises the federal Medicaid match by 3 percentage points for 16 quarters, then 2 and then 1, for states that use the money to raise nursing home staff wages and benefits, support retention, and improve care quality.
Expands the special focus facility program to cover at least 5 percent of facilities and adds on-site compliance consultation and training for struggling facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home and skilled nursing facility operators would bear new staffing, bonding, reporting, and audit costs, with smaller margins for facilities that run with fewer nurses or heavier administrative staffing. Home care providers would lose the ability to require arbitration. Taxpayers would fund the new programs, including a $1.3 billion building-modification and staff-investment demonstration, $570 million for survey improvements, $250 million for cost-report audits, and the higher federal Medicaid match.

drawbacks.text: The 24/7 registered nurse requirement, minimum ratios, and 40-hour infection preventionist standard would substantially raise operating costs for facilities, and some operators warned that such mandates are hard to meet amid nursing workforce shortages; the bill responds with rural and hardship waivers and federal wage funding rather than eliminating the requirements.

The bill appropriates or transfers well over $2 billion, including a $1.3 billion demonstration program, $570 million for survey improvements, and $250 million for cost-report audits, paid for by taxpayers and by transfers from the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund.
Minimum staffing ratios would be set through a study-then-regulation process rather than fixed in statute, so the final strength of the requirement would depend on future CMS decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to a uniquely vulnerable population: nursing home residents suffered heavily during COVID-19, and understaffing and forced arbitration are among the most documented problems in the sector. The main costs fall on an industry that historically operates on thin margins and would need to hire more nurses, though the bill pairs the toughest mandates with federal money for wages and hardship waivers for rural facilities. The design is more targeted than a pure mandate bill, but the price tag is real and the arbitration ban is a clear loss for facilities that rely on it to limit lawsuits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2021, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Nursing Home Improvement and Accountability Act of 2021 on August 10, 2021, joined by five Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
The Senate Finance Committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators, including corporate chains, kept their existing staffing levels, arbitration agreements, and reporting practices, with no new bonding or audit requirements.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. Support was entirely Democratic: Sen. Wyden and 5 of 48 Senate Democrats cosponsored; no Republican signed on, so the partisan shape is known only from the sponsor list.

industries.industry: Nursing home and skilled nursing facility operators
industries.note: The bill imposes real costs on operators: 24/7 registered nurse coverage, infection-prevention staffing, possible minimum ratios, a $500,000 surety bond, penalties for false staffing data, cost-report audits, and an end to pre-dispute arbitration. It also channels a multi-year boost in federal Medicaid matching funds through facilities to raise staff wages and benefits, but the industry's core position was to keep the status quo, which meant weaker staffing standards and arbitration agreements stayed in place when the bill died.

industries.industry: Nursing home and long-term care workers
industries.note: The conditional federal Medicaid increase could be used only to raise staff wages and benefits, fund training, and reduce turnover, and staffing mandates would tend to increase demand for nurses and aides.

industries.industry: Home care and home health providers
industries.note: The arbitration ban extends to providers of home and community-based services and home health care under Medicaid, taking away a tool used to limit lawsuits by clients.
